explanations.answer: It gets trampled and eaten by birds
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The seed falls along the path, where it was trampled, and the birds of the air devoured it. I think that seed barely had time to look around. It's a rough ending, and Jesus doesn't dress it up.

explanations.answer: It sinks in and sprouts overnight
explanations.explanation: No sprouting on the path, friend. The text says the seed was trampled, and the birds of the air devoured it. Sprouting isn't what happens to that seed. I'd say it had the worst landing spot in the whole field.

explanations.answer: It washes away in the rain
explanations.explanation: Rain never shows up in this parable. What Jesus says is that the seed along the path was trampled, and the birds of the air devoured it. So the weather isn't what happens to this seed, the trampling and the birds are. I've had a cookie sheet go wrong in a lot of ways, but never by birds.
That's it, baker. The seedlings withered because they had no moisture. They did come up first, but the moisture was missing. A dough with no liquid in it does the same thing, it just crumbles.

Close to what you'd guess, but the text doesn't say sunlight. Jesus says the seedlings withered because they had no moisture. The seed on rocky ground did come up, so the trouble was what they couldn't drink. Even I wouldn't blame the oven light for this one.

Shade isn't mentioned in this story at all. Jesus says the seedlings on the rocky ground withered because they had no moisture. They came up, then dried out. I think a little shade would have been nice, but the text only talks about the moisture.

True, friend. The seed falls among thorns, and the thorns grow up with it and choke the seedlings. They weren't just nearby, they grew up right alongside. Imagine trying to stretch out with a crowd of thorns in the same pot, I'd have no room for my mustache.

That one's actually true. Jesus says the seed fell among thorns, which grew up with it and choked the seedlings. The thorns didn't stay in their own corner, they grew up right alongside. So this seed got crowded out the whole way up.
A hundredfold, baker! The seed on good soil sprang up and produced a crop, and Jesus says it's a hundredfold. One seed turning into a hundred. If my dough did that, I'd need a bigger planet.
Thirty? Friend, thirty would already have me dancing on my gold base. But in Luke, Jesus says the crop from the good soil is a hundredfold. A HUNDRED! My best batch ever just got embarrassed.
Sixty is a lot, but Luke gives a bigger number. Jesus says the seed on good soil produced a crop, a hundredfold. That's one seed, a hundred times over. I'd have to count twice just to believe it.
That's right. His disciples asked Him what the parable meant. They went straight to the One who told it. I think that's the smartest move anybody makes in this whole scene.
Nobody asks about directions, friend. The disciples asked Jesus what the parable meant. The field is just where the story happens, and the question goes to the meaning. No map needed for this one.

It's a fair thing to wonder, but that's not what they ask. The text says His disciples asked Him what the parable meant. They wanted the whole thing explained, not one detail of it. Good news is, He answers.

It's the other way around, friend. Jesus says, “The knowledge of the mysteries of the kingdom of God has been given to you…” So it was given to the disciples, not kept from them. The disciples asked, and they got an answer.

False is right. Jesus tells them, “The knowledge of the mysteries of the kingdom of God has been given to you…” Given, not kept back. Then He explains the parable to them, and says the seed is the word of God.

Yes, baker. Jesus says the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved. He names the one who does it. That's a serious line, and Jesus says it plainly.

Jesus doesn't name a false prophet here. He says the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts. Only one is named in the verse, and that's the devil. I'd make a terrible detective if I added a suspect the text never mentions.
Jesus doesn't point to any group in the crowd here. He says the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts. The one doing the taking is the devil, and that's the name in the verse.
Root, baker. Jesus says they hear the word and receive it with joy, but they have no root. They believe for a season, then fall away in the time of testing. Joy on top, nothing holding it down below.

The text doesn't say they lacked a teacher. Jesus says they receive the word with joy, but they have no root. That's the thing missing, and it shows when the time of testing comes. I think a root is something you can't see until you need it.

Friends aren't part of this picture. What Jesus says is that the people on the rocky ground receive the word with joy, but they have no root. Everything else sounds fine on the surface. The trouble is down underneath.
Not quite, friend. Jesus says they believe for a season, but in the time of testing, they fall away. So the testing is exactly where it breaks down. They started with joy, but they didn't stand firm.

False is right. Jesus says they believe for a season, but in the time of testing, they fall away. The joy was real at the start, and the root was what was missing. It's a sober line, and I'll leave it sober.

True, baker. Jesus says those among the thorns are choked by the worries, riches, and pleasures of this life. That's three things, and not one of them sounds like a villain. Ordinary stuff can be the very thing that chokes them, and Jesus says their fruit does not mature.

That's actually true. Jesus says they are choked by the worries, riches, and pleasures of this life. Worries, riches and pleasures, all three are in the verse. It's a list that fits a lot of ordinary Tuesdays, mine included.

That's it. Jesus says they hear the word, cling to it, and by persevering produce a crop. Hearing is the start, holding on is the next part. Think of it like a good dough you keep working until it's ready.

explanations.answer: Hear it once and move on
explanations.explanation: Hearing is only part of it, friend. Jesus says the good-soil people hear the word, cling to it, and by persevering produce a crop. Holding on is what He names for them.

The verse doesn't say that. Jesus says they hear the word, cling to it, and by persevering produce a crop. The picture is holding on and bearing fruit. Keeping it to themselves would be a different story entirely.
True, baker. Jesus says he sets it on a stand, so those who enter can see the light. A lamp's whole job is to be seen by the people walking in. Nobody lights one just to hide it.

That's true, actually. Jesus says he sets the lamp on a stand, so those who enter can see the light. Covering it with a jar or putting it under a bed is the thing He says no one does. The lamp goes up where everybody can use it.

explanations.answer: They will all be brought to light
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Jesus says, “…there is nothing hidden that will not be disclosed, and nothing concealed that will not be made known and brought to light.” Nothing is left out of that sentence. It's said twice, in two different ways.

Jesus says the opposite. He says, “…there is nothing hidden that will not be disclosed, and nothing concealed that will not be made known and brought to light.” Nothing hidden, nothing concealed, so none of it stays that way. That's a big "nothing" to sit with.

explanations.answer: They will fade and be forgotten
explanations.explanation: Forgotten isn't what He says. Jesus says, “…there is nothing hidden that will not be disclosed, and nothing concealed that will not be made known and brought to light.” These things come out into the open. Fading away isn't in the verse.
That's it, baker. Jesus says, “Pay attention, therefore, to how you listen.” Not only what you hear, but how you hear it. That's a good one to take with you out of the bakery.
That's not what He says. Jesus says, “Pay attention, therefore, to how you listen.” The focus is on the listening itself, not the seating chart. I'd have picked a spot near the oven anyway.
Travel doesn't come up here, friend. Jesus says, “Pay attention, therefore, to how you listen.” It's about how they hear, not how far they go. You can stay right where you are and still do it.

That's the one. Jesus says, “…whoever does not have, even what he thinks he has will be taken away from him.” It's a sobering line, and it comes right after He tells them to pay attention to how they listen. I think He wants every one of us to take that seriously.
Doubling isn't in the verse, friend. The first half says whoever has will be given more, not doubled. For the one who does not have, Jesus says even what he thinks he has will be taken away from him.

Protection isn't what Jesus says here. His words are, “…whoever does not have, even what he thinks he has will be taken away from him.” It's a firm line, and He gives it right after telling them to pay attention to how they listen. I'd say it's worth reading twice.
